F1.quote: is a global, radically participatory research initiative spanning nine countries across five continents. Here, data workers themselves become community researchers, identifying urgent issues, formulating their own questions, and choosing the formats that best tell their stories
F1.claim: the project's definition of itself: a global, radically participatory research initiative in nine countries on five continents, in which data workers become community researchers who identify the issues, set the questions and choose the formats
F1.lineage: what it is: data workers' own research in their workplaces

F2.quote: we created and developed Workers’ Inquiry as a Research Methodology or WIRM, a framework designed to turn hidden and precarious labor into a shared, politicized site for knowledge-making, public engagement, and tangible change.
F2.claim: the project names its method Workers' Inquiry as a Research Methodology (WIRM), a framework to turn hidden and precarious labor into a politicized site of knowledge-making, public engagement and change
F2.lineage: the method: a workers' inquiry after Marx (1880), WIRM, participatory action research

F3.quote: zines, documentaries, comics, essays, podcasts, and animations can be downloaded from the project repository
F3.claim: the inquiries are published as zines, documentaries, comics, essays, podcasts and animations, downloadable from the repository

F4.quote: 19 data workers in Venezuela, Kenya, Syria, Brazil, France and Germany conducting research with their colleagues in their respective workplaces and reporting on labor conditions and widespread practices in the AI industry.
F4.claim: 19 data workers in six named countries research labor conditions and practices in the AI industry with colleagues in their own workplaces
F4.lineage: scale: the inquirers and their countries

F5.locus: home, inquiry 'Impact of Remotasks’ Closure on Kenyan Workers' (Mophat Okinyi)
F5.quote: In March 2024, Remotasks shut down thousands of accounts of data workers in African countries.
F5.claim: an inquiry documents Remotasks shutting down thousands of African data workers' accounts in March 2024

F6.locus: home, inquiry 'Mental Health and Drug Dependency in Content Moderation' (Fasica Berhane Gebrekidan)
F6.quote: Exploited by subcontractors like Sama, Meta content moderators in Nairobi face psychological trauma and silencing.
F6.claim: an inquiry documents Meta content moderators in Nairobi, employed through subcontractors such as Sama, facing psychological trauma and silencing

F7.locus: home, inquiry 'The Impact of Gift Card Payments on MTurk Workers' (Alexis Chávez)
F7.quote: Amazon Mechanical Turk pays data workers with gift cards instead of money. This report underlines how this payment method fosters workers‘ dependency
F7.claim: an inquiry documents Amazon Mechanical Turk paying data workers in gift cards, and how the payment fosters dependency

F8.locus: home, inquiry 'Behind the Face of AI' (Clara and B)
F8.quote: This short comic details the experiences of data workers in France working for Scale AI as human chatbots. They explore what it is to be human and the consequences of acting like a machine.
F8.claim: an inquiry (a comic) documents data workers in France working for Scale AI as human chatbots, acting like a machine
F8.lineage: workers who perform as the machine

F9.locus: home, inquiry 'The Labor Behind AI Intimacy' (Michael Geoffrey Asia)
F9.quote: When users think they are talking to a machine, human emotion becomes data.
F9.claim: an inquiry on AI intimacy: where users think they talk to a machine, human emotion becomes data
F9.lineage: workers who perform as the machine

F10.locus: home, inquiry by James Mojez Oyange
F10.quote: “Just Send us Pictures of Your feet”: Consent and Biometric Extraction in the AI Supply Chain … The boundary between labour and personal resource has disappeared: the human body becomes raw material.
F10.claim: an inquiry on consent and biometric extraction in the AI supply chain: the worker's body becomes raw material
F10.lineage: consent and the extraction of workers' personal data

F11.locus: home, inquiries 'Data Workers Organizing: The African Content Moderators Union' (Richard Mathenge) and 'Organizing Across Borders' (Joan Kinyua)
F11.quote: This documentary explores the issues faced by data workers at Sama in Nairobi, Kenya, that led to the union’s creation. … A Partnership Between the Data Workers Inquiry and the Data Labelers Association.
F11.claim: inquiries document the issues that led to the African Content Moderators Union and a partnership with the Data Labelers Association

F12.locus: home, inquiry 'Unveiling: The Invisible Lives of TikTok Data Workers in London' (Fasica Berhane Gebrekidan)
F12.quote: They face systematic outsourcing, replacement by inadequate automated systems, and layoffs without accountability.
F12.claim: an inquiry documents TikTok trust and safety workers in London facing outsourcing, replacement by automated systems and layoffs

F13.quote: Artists, translators, writers, nurses, and internet users produce data for AI without compensation.
F13.claim: invited pieces extend data work to artists, translators, writers, nurses and internet users who produce data for AI without compensation
F13.lineage: whose labor: data work that enables AI systems

F14.quote: We are the organizing team developing a methodology and a platform for data workers to conduct individual inquiries. We provide guidance and training in specific data collection and analysis methods, and constantly monitor the legal and ethical boundaries of the inquiries.
F14.claim: the organizing team develops the method and platform, trains the workers in data collection and analysis, and monitors the inquiries' legal and ethical boundaries

F15.locus: home, inquiry 'Life of a Latin American Data Worker' (Oskarina Veronica Fuentes Anaya)
F15.quote: Irregular working hours, uncertainty, meager wages, and unpaid time are daily realities for platform data workers.
F15.claim: an inquiry documents irregular hours, uncertainty, meager wages and unpaid time for platform data workers in Latin America

F16.quote: The project brings to light the lived realities of workers in content moderation, data annotation, and other essential yet precarious roles that keep AI systems running.
F16.claim: DAIR's page: the project brings to light the lived realities of workers in content moderation, annotation and other precarious roles that keep AI systems running
F16.lineage: whose labor: data work that enables AI systems

F17.locus: Workers’ Inquiry as a Research Methodology ¶1 s1
F17.quote: Across the board, the project channels Marx’s 1880 Workers’ Inquiry, reframing data work under AI as a capital-laden terrain of exploitation, struggle, and possibility, one that is ripe for solidarity, collective organizing, and structured resistance.
F17.claim: the project channels Marx's 1880 Workers' Inquiry and reframes data work under AI as a terrain of exploitation, struggle and possibility, ripe for organizing
F17.lineage: the method: a workers' inquiry after Marx (1880), WIRM, participatory action research

F18.locus: Workers’ Inquiry as a Research Methodology ¶1 s2
F18.quote: which moves beyond documentation toward a participatory, worker-led process that centers workers’ epistemic authority, fosters self-expression, and strengthens organizing capacity.
F18.claim: WIRM moves beyond documentation to a worker-led process that centers workers' epistemic authority and strengthens organizing capacity

F19.quote: I didn’t want to speak for or about data workers anymore. I wanted to build a space where they could tell their own stories, and where research was a form of collective thinking and organizing, not extraction.
F19.claim: the research lead: a space where workers tell their own stories and research is collective thinking and organizing, not extraction

F20.locus: More Work, 'Workers’ Inquiry as a Research Methodology'
F20.quote: Our paper detailing the Workers’ Inquiry as a Research Methodology or WIRM methodology we designed that underpins the DWI was accepted to AIES.
F20.claim: the WIRM paper that underpins the project was accepted to AIES
F20.lineage: the method: a workers' inquiry after Marx (1880), WIRM, participatory action research

F21.quote: In Kenya, workers from Sama, CloudFactory, and Remotasks are organizing to demand fair treatment and better conditions.
F21.claim: workers from Sama, CloudFactory and Remotasks in Kenya are organizing for fair treatment and better conditions

F22.quote: A panel of data workers organized by us in collaboration with MEPs testified at the European Parliament on February 22, 2024. Their input directly influenced the negotiations leading to the adoption of the Platform Workers’ Directive
F22.claim: a panel of data workers organized by the project testified at the European Parliament on 22 February 2024, and DAIR states it influenced the Platform Workers' Directive

F23.quote: We supported the Data Labelers Association's creation and launch.
F23.claim: the project supported the creation and launch of the Data Labelers Association

F24.quote: Three of our community researchers, Richard Mathenge Mophat Okinyi, and Kauna Malgwi went on to be named in the TIME 100 most influential people in AI.
F24.claim: three community researchers were named in the TIME 100 most influential people in AI

F25.locus: card snippet (Instagram unreachable: HTTP 429, login redirect)
F25.quote: Project: Data Workers' Inquiry (DWI) community-based research exposing hidden, precarious labor behind AI and digital platforms.
F25.claim: the card: community-based research exposing hidden, precarious labor behind AI and digital platforms

F26.locus: card title (YouTube, Weizenbaum-Institut, video 2m; unreachable: HTTP 429, bot check)
F26.quote: The Data Workers' Inquiry - Unveiling the Hidden Labor Behind AI
F26.claim: the Weizenbaum Institute's video presents the project as unveiling the hidden labor behind AI

F27.quote: The Distributed AI Research Institute, or DAIR—which seeks to conduct community-rooted AI research that is independent from the technology industry—has launched a new project called the Data Workers' Inquiry to invite data workers to create their own research and recount their experiences. The project is supported by DAIR, the Weizenbaum Institute, and TU Berlin.
F27.claim: Tech Policy Press: DAIR launched the project to invite data workers to create their own research; it is supported by DAIR, the Weizenbaum Institute and TU Berlin

F28.locus: transcript, Milagros Miceli at the launch
F28.quote: I think the idea of the Data Workers' Inquiry is to provide a platform in which the workers speak for themselves. They create the research questions, they design the research questions, they design the investigation that they want to conduct in their workplaces with their co-workers.
F28.claim: Miceli: a platform in which the workers speak for themselves, create the questions and design the investigation with their co-workers

F29.quote: One of the things multiple researchers have brought up is that data workers are bound by non-disclosure agreements, which makes it especially risky for them to speak out.
F29.claim: data workers are bound by non-disclosure agreements, which makes speaking out risky
F29.lineage: non-disclosure agreements and the risk of speaking

F30.quote: The idea of a worker's inquiry goes back to 1880 actually with Karl Marx. … Now Marx's original inquiry was basically just a survey of 100 questions for workers about the nuts and bolts of their jobs, wages, cost of living, contracts, and so on.
F30.claim: the workers' inquiry goes back to Marx in 1880, a survey of 100 questions on jobs, wages, cost of living and contracts
F30.lineage: the method: a workers' inquiry after Marx (1880), WIRM, participatory action research

F31.quote: For this episode, journalist and audio producer Rebecca Rand parsed some of the ideas and experiences discussed at a virtual launch event for the inquiry that took place earlier this month.
F31.claim: the launch event was held earlier in the month of the 28 July 2024 episode

F32.quote: this is dangerous work, particularly for the workers because some of the workers that are involved in this project are actually still working in these companies and there'll be consequences for them
F32.claim: Dinika: the work is dangerous for the workers, some still employed by the companies they research
F32.lineage: non-disclosure agreements and the risk of speaking

F33.quote: Data Workers’ Inquiry is a community-centered project in which data workers join us as community researchers to lead their own inquiry in their respective workplaces. Our methodology aims to deepen the tradition of community-based participatory research by empowering data workers to guide the direction of the research, such that it is oriented towards their needs and goals of building workplace power, but supported by formally trained qualitative researchers.
F33.claim: the project's LinkedIn page: data workers lead their own inquiry in their workplaces, the method deepening community-based participatory research toward building workplace power, supported by trained qualitative researchers
F33.lineage: what it is: data workers' own research in their workplaces

F34.quote: why are data workers asked to share their faces, voices, and even photos of their children as part of their jobs? After speaking with nine workers in Kenya, a troubling pattern emerged. Workers were not only giving their labour to build AI systems, but they were also giving away deeply personal data, often with no clear purpose given, no informed consent obtained, and no idea where any of that data ends up.
F34.claim: Oyange's inquiry: workers in Kenya are asked for their faces, voices and photos of their children, giving personal data without clear purpose or informed consent
F34.lineage: consent and the extraction of workers' personal data

F35.quote: Mojez documents what firms in the AI supply chain collect from the people who annotate their data: facial footage, identity documents, keystrokes, screen recordings and images made inside their own homes.
F35.claim: the report documents firms collecting facial footage, identity documents, keystrokes, screen recordings and images from inside annotators' homes
F35.lineage: consent and the extraction of workers' personal data

F36.quote: This year, Data Workers' Inquiry received an Award of Distinction as part of the Prix Ars Electronica, recognizing the project’s diverse forms of output and the ways data workers use them to document and communicate their experiences.
F36.claim: the project received an Award of Distinction of the Prix Ars Electronica (2026)

F37.quote: Our new project Data Workers United is a move from investigating to action. This partnership between The Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) and SUPERRR Lab will build a network that strengthens solidarity across movements and borders.
F37.claim: the project's successor, Data Workers United (DAIR with SUPERRR Lab), moves from investigating to action

F38.quote: You, me, and anyone with internet access do unpaid, uncredited data work to feed AI models.
F38.claim: Miceli: anyone with internet access does unpaid, uncredited data work that feeds AI models
F38.lineage: whose labor: data work that enables AI systems

F39.locus: post by Ares Biescas (reposted, 4d), on Horacio Espinosa
F39.quote: Now he says something else weighs on him: without the workers knowing it, the labelling they did was helping to train the AI systems that now take part in that same moderation work. Despite the NDA he signed, he has decided to speak out after finding support in Data Workers’ Inquiry, a Berlin-based organisation that coordinates a global network of data workers and researches the human labour that makes AI work.
F39.claim: EFE's interview: moderators' labelling trained the AI that now moderates; the project described as a Berlin-based organisation coordinating a global network of data workers and researching the human labour that makes AI work
F39.lineage: workers who perform as the machine

F40.quote: The Data Workers’ Inquiry is a community-based research project in which data workers conduct research in their workplaces. The findings serve as a repository and resource for researchers, journalists, and policymakers seeking first-hand accounts of data work, as well as for other data workers.
F40.claim: the Weizenbaum Institute's definition: a community-based research project in which data workers research their workplaces, its findings a repository of first-hand accounts for researchers, journalists, policymakers and other data workers
F40.lineage: what it is: data workers' own research in their workplaces

F41.quote: behind the glossy veneer of AI-powered applications and services lies a hidden workforce of data workers who form the backbone of this technological revolution. These workers, often located in the Global South, are tasked with the labor-intensive and emotionally taxing work of data annotation, content moderation, and other forms of data processing that enable AI systems to function.
F41.claim: behind AI applications lies a hidden workforce of data workers, often in the Global South, doing annotation, moderation and other data processing that enables AI systems

F42.quote: Despite their critical role in the development and maintenance of AI, data workers are often rendered invisible, their contributions unrecognized, and their well-being overlooked. This is by design, and not accidental. So far, it has been common practice to speak and research about data workers, instead of speaking or researching with them.
F42.claim: data workers are rendered invisible by design; research has been about them, not with them

F43.quote: The team of researchers led by Dr. Miceli, Adio Dinika, Krystal Kauffmann, Camilla Wagner, and Laurenz Sachenbacher, has brought together 15 co-researchers from Venezuela, Kenya, Syria, and Germany and employment contexts, including content moderators and data annotators working for various outsourcing companies and platforms.
F43.claim: the team led by Miceli, with Dinika, Kauffmann, Wagner and Sachenbacher, brought together 15 co-researchers from Venezuela, Kenya, Syria and Germany
F43.lineage: scale: the inquirers and their countries

F44.quote: Drawing inspiration from Marx's 1880 “Workers Inquiry”, the Data Workers Inquiry employs a participatory action research (PAR) methodology, which emphasizes the collaboration between researchers and members of directly affected communities to understand and change problematic situations
F44.claim: drawing on Marx's 1880 Workers' Inquiry, the project employs participatory action research, the collaboration of researchers with directly affected communities
F44.lineage: the method: a workers' inquiry after Marx (1880), WIRM, participatory action research

F45.quote: These accounts show how outsourcing companies prey on vulnerable populations, such as refugees, offering them work with little compensation.
F45.claim: the accounts show outsourcing companies preying on vulnerable populations such as refugees, with little compensation

F46.quote: Duration : August 2023 - November 2024 … Partners : Weizenbaum-Institut, TU Berlin, DAIR Institut
F46.claim: the Weizenbaum project ran August 2023 to November 2024, with the Weizenbaum Institute, TU Berlin and DAIR as partners

F47.quote: In 1880, Karl Marx initiated the Workers’ Inquiry, a novel and unprecedented research project, inviting industrial workers to participate in producing first-hand accounts of the capitalist system and their place within it. The ‘Data Worker’s Inquiry’ is a renewal of this project for the age of AI.
F47.claim: Sachenbacher (Bot Populi): the project is a renewal of Marx's 1880 Workers' Inquiry for the age of AI
F47.lineage: the method: a workers' inquiry after Marx (1880), WIRM, participatory action research

F48.quote: Data work refers to an essential occupation of digital capitalism that amounts to between 4.4% and 12.5% of the global labor force.
F48.claim: data work is an occupation amounting to between 4.4% and 12.5% of the global labor force
F48.lineage: whose labor: data work that enables AI systems

F49.quote: scholars distinguish between three subtypes in the AI development pipeline—AI preparation, AI impersonation, and AI verification—and content moderation
F49.claim: scholars distinguish AI preparation, AI impersonation and AI verification in the AI pipeline, and content moderation
F49.lineage: workers who perform as the machine

F50.quote: The point is for workers to retain epistemic authority, to center their perspectives on the struggles they face in following the overarching goals of the organization and building workplace power. Assisted by a core team of trained qualitative researchers, each of the 13 projects was tailored to the specificities of their respective national context
F50.claim: workers retain epistemic authority, assisted by a core team; each of 13 projects was tailored to its national context

F51.quote: Marx’s original 100 questions were adapted in iterative cycles to account for the new modes of production, new forms of technological involvement, and new forms of global competition
F51.claim: Marx's 100 questions were adapted in iterative cycles to new modes of production and technology
F51.lineage: the method: a workers' inquiry after Marx (1880), WIRM, participatory action research

F52.quote: Through this dependency, the workers are also politically disempowered, exacerbated by so-called ‘Non-disclosure agreements’ (NDAs) that legally prohibit workers in BPOs from voicing their contempt and hence from collectivizing.
F52.claim: NDAs legally prohibit workers in BPOs from voicing complaint and so from collectivizing
F52.lineage: non-disclosure agreements and the risk of speaking

F53.quote: Testimonies of workers reported mass rejections or unsubstantiated suspensions of platform accounts based on allegedly inaccurate task completion, which amounts to the aforementioned institutionalized wage theft
F53.claim: workers' testimonies report mass rejections and unsubstantiated account suspensions, amounting to institutionalized wage theft

F54.quote: consider the case of Remotask in Kenya, which closed all its operations, allegedly in response to workers’ organizing, threatening many with economic ruin.
F54.claim: Remotasks closed all its operations in Kenya, allegedly in response to workers' organizing

F55.quote: which had direct effects concerning, for example, the ‘Platform workers’ Directive’ of the European Union, which included data work in its definition of platform work after testimonies of Data Workers invited by researchers.
F55.claim: the EU Platform Workers' Directive included data work in its definition of platform work after data workers' testimonies

F56.quote: However, all the solution approaches we accompanied and enthusiastically applaud, such as efforts to build workers’ councils, advocacy groups, or non-institutionalized solidarity structures in the form of peer-to-peer mental health support, were largely forced to remain on a localized level.
F56.claim: a core researcher's stated limit: the organizing efforts the project accompanied were largely forced to remain local

F57.quote: it also highlights the lurking danger of listening to invisibilized, precarious workers only after someone allegedly important shifts attention onto them. We, in the core team, further observed a growing tendency amongst academics to somewhat ‘fetishize’ workers’ perspectives
F57.claim: a core researcher's stated limit: the danger of hearing workers only through institutional attention, and academics' tendency to fetishize workers' perspectives

F58.locus: ¶ 'Celebrating the launch of the Data Workers Inquiry Project'
F58.quote: The project is a global and radically participatory research initiative that lets data workers themselves become community researchers. It is led by Weizenbaum Institute researcher and our close collaborator, Dr. Milagros Miceli.
F58.claim: SUPERRR: a global, radically participatory initiative led by Milagros Miceli
F58.lineage: what it is: data workers' own research in their workplaces

F59.quote: the initiative doesn’t reduce data workers to research subjects but empowers them to be community researchers by providing them with fair wages, a methodology, and a platform to conduct their own individual inquiries.
F59.claim: the initiative pays the community researchers fair wages and gives them a method and a platform

F60.quote: working in a job where he and other workers impersonate an AI sex chatbot
F60.claim: an inquiry by a worker who, with others, impersonates an AI sex chatbot
F60.lineage: workers who perform as the machine

F61.locus: SEPTEMBER – Organizing the Data Workers Transnational Assembly in Berlin
F61.quote: Most data workers have to sign Non-Disclosure Agreements that prohibit them from speaking about their projects or the tasks that they completed, making it almost impossible to prove their work experience and expertise
F61.claim: most data workers sign NDAs that bar them from speaking of their tasks, making their expertise hard to prove
F61.lineage: non-disclosure agreements and the risk of speaking

F62.locus: SEPTEMBER – Organizing the Data Workers Transnational Assembly in Berlin ¶1
F62.quote: Together with the Data Workers Inquiry, we organized the Data Worker Transnational Assembly that took place in Berlin.
F62.claim: SUPERRR and the project organized the Data Worker Transnational Assembly in Berlin (September 2025)

F63.quote: The Distributed Artificial Intelligence Research Institute partners wi...
F63.claim: a Democracy Now video on TikTok: DAIR partners with … (title truncated on the card)

F64.locus: card title (Facebook, DW Stories, video 22:12; URL not found)
F64.quote: Behind today's AI revolution stands an invisible workforce: millions of data ...
F64.claim: a DW Stories video: an invisible workforce of millions of data [workers] behind the AI revolution (title truncated on the card)

F65.quote: PRESS RELEASE: The Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) and Weizenbaum Institute launch the Data Worker’s Inquiry repository and talk series.
F65.claim: DAIR and the Weizenbaum Institute launch the repository and a talk series
F65.date: 2024-07 (launch event 8 July, the year from B5)

F66.quote: The Data Workers’ Inquiry is a community-based research project in which data workers from all over the world conduct individual inquiries. From reports and animations to powerful documentaries and zines, the Data Workers‘ Inquiry repository presents a multifaceted view of the realities confronted by data workers, ranging from psychological, physical, and sexual abuse, to resistance strategies and efforts to unionize.
F66.claim: the press release's definition, and the repository's range, from psychological, physical and sexual abuse to resistance and unionizing
F66.date: 2024-07 (launch event 8 July, the year from B5)

F67.quote: The data workers who are tasked with the labor-intensive and emotionally taxing work of data labeling, content moderation, and other forms of data processing that enable AI systems to function, are often located in the Global Majority, precariously employed, and politically dispersed. The Data Workers’ Inquiry provides a platform for them to conduct their own research and describe issues in their own words.
F67.claim: data workers doing labeling, moderation and other processing that enables AI are often in the Global Majority, precarious and politically dispersed; the project gives them a platform for their own research
F67.lineage: whose labor: data work that enables AI systems

F68.quote: This community-based research project has brought together 15 data workers from Kenya, Venezuela, Syria, Lebanon, and Germany, and diverse employment contexts, including various outsourcing companies and platforms. The data workers develop unique research questions, design and conduct their inquiries, and prepare a presentation format for their findings.
F68.claim: 15 data workers from Kenya, Venezuela, Syria, Lebanon and Germany at launch; they set the questions, conduct the inquiries and choose the format
F68.lineage: scale: the inquirers and their countries

F69.quote: We center their experiences and recognize their unique knowledge. We are proactive supporters, but the epistemic authority remains with the workers.
F69.claim: Miceli: the team supports; epistemic authority remains with the workers

F70.quote: The project repository is a valuable resource for researchers, journalists, and policymakers seeking first-hand accounts of data work … The findings are an urgent call to confront labor inequities and exploitative practices.
F70.claim: the repository serves researchers, journalists and policymakers; Dinika: the findings call for confronting labor inequities

F71.quote: The launch event will take place online on Monday, July 8th, 8:00 AM PT / 11:00 AM EST / 5 PM CET.
F71.claim: the online launch event, Monday 8 July
